nameStory: The fieldfare gets its name from its love of open fields and farmland, where it forages for food during winter months. The "fare" part comes from an old English word meaning "to go" or "to travel," perfectly describing this bird's migratory lifestyle as it journeys from northern breeding grounds to southern wintering areas.
description: The fieldfare is a large, striking thrush about 10 inches long - roughly the size of an American Robin but more boldly patterned. This European visitor sports a distinctive gray head and rump that contrast beautifully with its brown back and heavily spotted, rust-washed breast. While extremely rare in New England with only 3 recorded sightings, fieldfares are strong migrants that occasionally stray across the Atlantic during their winter wanderings.

idTips.label: Gray head and rump
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive slate-gray coloring on the head, neck, and rump that contrasts sharply with the brown back - this gray "cap and tail" pattern is unique among New England thrushes

idTips.label: Heavily spotted breast
idTips.description: The breast shows bold, dark spotting over a warm reddish-orange wash, creating a more dramatic pattern than the subtle spots of most thrushes you'd see here

idTips.label: White underwings
idTips.description: In flight, watch for bright white patches under the wings that flash conspicuously - a field mark that helps distinguish it from our native thrushes

idTips.label: Large size
idTips.description: Noticeably larger and more robust than most thrushes, with a sturdy build that makes it appear almost robin-like in proportions

idTips.label: Chattering calls
idTips.description: Listen for harsh, guttural "chuck-chuck-chuck" calls and chattering sounds quite different from the melodious songs of American Robins

habitat: In their rare New England appearances, fieldfares have been spotted in open areas with scattered trees, agricultural fields, and suburban parks - habitats similar to where American Robins forage. They prefer areas with berry-producing trees and shrubs for winter feeding, often near farmland or large grassy spaces.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to be seen as fieldfares would be heading back to northern European breeding grounds. Any spring sighting would be exceptional.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during breeding season, as they nest in northern Europe and Asia. Any summer record would be extraordinarily rare.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for a New England sighting as migrating birds occasionally get blown off course. Look in berry-rich areas and mixed flocks with robins.
seasonality.winter: Most likely season for vagrant fieldfares to appear, often associating with American Robin flocks in areas with abundant winter berries and fruits.

funFact: Fieldfares have a unique defense strategy - they nest in small colonies and when threatened by predators like crows, the entire colony will dive-bomb the intruder while defecating on it, literally covering their enemies in bird droppings!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with an American Robin due to similar size and spotted breast, but remember "Gray Cap, Brown Back" - the fieldfare's gray head and rump with brown back is the opposite of a robin's dark head with gray back. The fieldfare's breast spots are also much bolder and more extensive.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "fieldfare," this is not a year-round field bird but rather a forest-nesting species that only uses fields for winter foraging. The extremely low sighting count means any fieldfare in New England would likely be a vagrant blown off course during migration - making it a potential "life bird" for even experienced birders.
compareHints: Compared to its cousin the American Robin, fieldfares have that distinctive gray head contrasting with a brown (not gray) back, much heavier breast spotting, and white underwing patches. They're also larger and more heavily built than robins, with harsher, more guttural calls rather than the robin's cheerful song.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While two other Turdus species (Redwing and Fieldfare) occasionally appear in New England as rare vagrants, American Robin is easily distinguished by its solid orange breast - the others have streaked or spotted underparts.
Unlike its cousin the American Robin, which has a solid rusty-red breast, the Redwing has rusty-red only on its wings and flanks with a spotted white breast.
